feedback.body:
Here I am, sorry for the delay.

As Ryan said, there is an ongoing work to deeply restructure the way settings are VFO state are saved: the old NVM APIs to read and write settings and VFO is going to be deprecated in the upcoming v0.5.0 release in favor of using the new NVM access functions based on devices and partitions. The code doing the actual read/write of settings and VFO is now common to all the platforms, which only need to provide the device(s) and partition(s) where data is stored.
The work is now in the [`settings-vfo-persistence`](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/tree/settings-vfo-persistence) branch and I hope to mainline it soon. It already works (tested a bit on linux, MD-380 and CS7000) but I still need to finish the support for Module17 and, more important, to test everything thoroughly on all the devices I have.

For the C62, I suggested to wait until this work gets mainlined (I think by the end of the month, but possibly before) so that the job is done only once and forever. We'll need to declare a device and partition table using the `flash_zephyr` driver, using the eeep driver as an intermediate layer to manage the flash pages (like in MD-380, for example). An intermediate step can be merging this PR as-is marking the commits as WIP and update the implementation once the new system is ready.

The issue with the C62 not saving data in `platform_terminate` will pop out on other devices as well (like Module17 rev. D), so having a unified approach is definitely a good idea. Also, it can be put in place on all the devices, even if they have a means to detect when the power is being turned off.
The new functions to write settings and VFO state already implement the skipping of unchanged data, so we just need to implement the part that calls those functions cyclically. To be decided whether we want to move the logic checking if something actually changed outside `settings_save` and `vfo_save` or keep it implicit. In either case, I'd go for a solution calculating some sort of hash of the data (the CCITT CRC or even something faster) rather than keeping multiple copies of the same data structure and compare them: these data structures are quite big (or will become big soon), and we may have to change the approach in the future because the RAM usage exceeds the amount available on some microcontrollers.

We can do in this way: replace commit [2ac74b0](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/commit/2ac74b060527bc2e95110e9e280e1e31197a4936) with the one bringing in the debounce logic on settings and VFO. Then I'll merge the PR to enable persistence on the C62 and cherry pick the debounce commit in `settings-vfo-persistence` to use it everywhere. Once the new settings system is done, I'll rebase the `Retevis-c62` branch on top of master and then we can creating another PR to update the NVM implementation.

+
+- Every function carries its module as a prefix: `history_insert`, `input_getDtmfChar`, `aprsPktList_init`, `vfo_load`. Functions without the prefix get sent back (#306, #340, #367, #396, #456).
+- Drivers are named `<peripheral><Chip>` — `spiStm32`, `adcStm32`, `flashStm32`, `adcHrc7000`. Name the driver after the silicon it talks to, never after the radio that happens to use it first: the next target will reuse it (#403, #498). Files are snake_case `<peripheral>_<chip>.c`: `adc_stm32f4.c`, `flash_stm32.c`, `gpio_bk4819.c` (#534).
+- All build-time feature and hardware macros use the `CONFIG_` prefix, matching `CONFIG_RTC`, `CONFIG_GPS`, `CONFIG_DISPLAY`. Not a bare name (#426, #492). `PLATFORM_<TARGET>` is the one exception: it identifies the target being built (#510).
+- Name a `CONFIG_` macro for what it configures, not for the first thing that used it: `CONFIG_CODEC_ENCODE_GAIN`, not `CONFIG_MIC_GAIN`, because codec2 accepts any input stream (#442).
+- Names describe what a thing *is*, not the container it currently sits in or the operation currently performed on it: `struct MessageSource` over `struct MessageListEntry`, `struct hdlcFrame` over `struct frame`, `ui_printAprsPkt` over `ui_drawAprsPkt` (you do not *draw* a packet), `testSyncword` over `trySync` (we are already synchronised; we are testing) (#396, #417, #492).
+- Prefer the shorter name when it is not ambiguous: `sample`, not `processSingleSample`; `multiKeyEvent`, not `multiKeyEventInProgress`; `snapshotSize`, not `snapshotLens` (#306, #417, #492).
+- Operation tables are named `<thing>_ops`, kernel-style: `struct message_ops` (#492).
+
+### Types and Data Structures
+
+- **Do not `typedef` a `struct` or an `enum`.** They are types already. Write `struct address`, not `address_t`. Reserve `typedef` for types that are not structs or enums. The codebase still contains many old typedefs and they are being removed progressively; do not add new ones. See the [kernel typedef guidance](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v5.6/process/coding-style.html#typedefs) (#340, #396, #481).
+- Use an `enum` (or `enum class` in C++) instead of a group of related `#define`s — for symbol IDs, chip command sets, register values, state codes, sector sizes (#165, #360, #362, #467, #498). A bitfield may legitimately be assigned from an enum; see `settings.h`'s `display_timer` (#360).

feedback.body: Can we assume that the power varies linearly (or quadratically) with the PWM value? If so, here we can use `power` to interpolate again between `low` and `high` and return the correct PWM value. This is going to be useful when OpenRTX will allow to have more than just two power settings.

feedback.body: How messy is it going to be to register/unregister message sources when entering/exiting from a given operating mode?

replies.author: turnrye
replies.body:
It wouldn't be that messy, but I'm not sure yet that it's what we'd want to do. Right now the registry already gates by the current mode. `messages_task(mode)` and `findSource(mode)` mean a source that isn't for the active mode is just inactive, so there's nothing to unregister on a switch. With a single source, registering once at init comes out identical to doing it per-opmode, so I've kept the simple version here.

Even with more protocols I'd lean toward leaving them registered rather than toggling on every mode enter/exit. My thought is, the sources are tiny and stateless. Why do more state transition etc than needed. 

The thing I do think deserves a cleanup by then is what you've flagged here; having each opmode own its registration (registered as it comes up) would read a lot cleaner than a stack of #ifs in the thread. I can do that now, or we can do it once APRS (and APRS-over-M17) get added.

replies.author: turnrye
replies.body:
Rather than register/unregister per mode, I kept the sources passthroughl. They don't keep any buffers of their own. M17 SMS just reads out of the packet on the way in and writes into the registry's buffer on the way out, so there's nothing per-source to allocate or free when the mode changes.

And the inbox storage only exists while a messaging mode is active, so sources don't stack up at startup. I think we should plan to hold APRS to the same bar and only add a shared buffer if it really needs one.

feedback.body:
Apart from code cleanliness, dynamic registration will allow each message source to allocate/release memory resources if needed. Now we do not need it, but in the future it may be the case, and it may happen that having multiple message sources being initialized at startup exhaust the RAM even if there is enough memory to run each of them individually. As usual, I tend towards future-proofing :smile: 

But if you say that is good enough :tm: for the time being, we can keep it as it is.

feedback.body:
General comments:

- the message dispatcher ended up being pretty simple: I think we can move the logic directly inside the "messages" module and make the "process_rx" and "format_tx" two message callbacks alongside the others (which I saw in the previous PR). Doing so will also squeeze the code size a bit more.
- the general naming convention for functions in OpenRTX is moduleName_functionName: this should be used also here.
- for large buffers I'd use dynamic memory allocation whenever possible: given that we allocate/release large blocks of memory, the fragmentation should not be a real issue. Dynamic memory allocation allows us to use the RAM more efficiently: if all the buffers are static, we pay for them at compile time and we'll run out of memory faster than expected. The radios based on STM32F4x allocate .bss and .data in the 64kB CCM RAM, while the heap goes in the large 128kB RAM. More in general, given that messages is something which may be used, a "pay for what you effectively use" approach works better. This is just a general indication, we then need to find the best way to implement this principle.

A clarification about dynamic memory allocation: the idea is to allocate memory when switching to an opmode which supports messages and release it when changing to something else. It may happen to have a back-to-back release/allocate pattern, but is fine.
For the pool of message bodies you can use `size_t` everywhere, to avoid casting.

feedback.body: Do you think it does make sense to create a [gpio device](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/master/openrtx/include/peripherals/gpio.h) for the BK4819 GPIOS?

The idea is to have a `bk4812_gpio.c` file providing an implementation of the GPIO API for the on-chip GPIOs (like [this](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/Retevis-c62/platform/drivers/GPIO/gpio_shiftReg.c), for example).
Then in `bk4812.h` (or in a dedicated header file), you have the macro that allows to declare a BK4812 GPIO driver instance:
```
#define GPIO_BK4812_DEVICE_DEFINE(name, bk4819Dev) \
extern const struct gpioApi gpioBk4819_ops;        \
const struct gpioDev name =                        \
{                                                  \
    .api  = &gpioBk4819_ops,                       \
    .priv = &bk4819Dev                             \
};
```
Given that you have to implement the setMode/set/clear GPIO functions in any case, this solution is going to cost only some more bytes of flash (all the structs are `static const`, and they end up there).

```suggestion
    uint8_t active_low;         ///< Per-pin active-low mask
```


+void platform_set_display_brightness(uint8_t brightness_percent)
+{
+    // Calculate duty cycle (1000us period = 1kHz)
+    uint32_t period_us = 1000; // 1kHz PWM frequency
+    uint32_t adjusted_brightness_percent = 0;

+    if (brightness_percent > 0) {

I think battery charge pin should not be used for this as it will indicate charging also when power button is switched on. Maybe better as you suggested to check battery voltage. As far as I remember battery voltage reads < 1V when power button is switched off and charging is active.
There is currently no UI for charging, I guess that's why MD-9600 is in the busy loop.
What is the expected behavior for MD-9600 when platform_pwrButtonStatus() returns false? main() function finishes and then MCU reboot and waits for battery voltage? 1. Checking for < 3V will detect power button off while charging. (When using < 1V it won't be responsive)

I will provide together with the battery PR.

feedback.body:
> What is the expected behavior for MD-9600 when platform_pwrButtonStatus() returns false? main() function finishes and then MCU reboot and waits for battery voltage? If yes, then C62 might require a software reset after leaving main() and I have to check from when the battery voltage reading code would work.

The MD-9600 is a vehicular radio, with no battery. However is made such that the MCU is powered directly from the 12V input and always on, hence the busy loop. When `main()` returns the MCU restarts and it falls in the busy loop waiting for a power button press.
If you can have a fixup commit which removes all the stuff, it'd be nice. Then you add another one adding the new configuration, in this way the commit history stays clean and easily bisectable.

> When testing I recognised that the SW will hang when trying to transmit in M17 mode. As it is anyway not supported in this PR I suggest adding a fixup to disable M17 (remove/comment #define CONFIG_M17)?

Yes, please :)

For the SPI interface, please use the [OpenRTX SPI driver API](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/master/openrtx/include/peripherals/spi.h) to make the driver re-usable in other devices as well. You can find an example on how to use the API in the W25Qx driver.

This will need to create a wrapper for the Zephyr SPI device, but it should be an easy task. Then, if the only possibility is to use a bitbanged SPI, you can instantiate a [SPI bitbang device](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/samples/drivers/spi_bitbang/README.html) using the Zephyr driver.

Thanks for the PR!
Do you mind splitting it in more commits, please? Each commit should be a distinct, complete change touching a specific part. I'd have the following commits:
- glue code for HR_C7000 hardware (glue code, RTC, ADC, GPIO driver)
- HD2 platform support (hwconfig, main, platform.c, CMakelists, ...)
- display and backlight
- keyboard
- GPS

Also, the subfolder under MCU should be HR_C7000: CSKY_V2 is the architecture. The same is for `hd2_regs.h`: it should go under `mcu/HR_C7000` and calling it `registers.h` should suffice. For that, instead of having a list of `#define` directives with macros, you can create a struct with the list of registers and then cast the base address of the peripheral. See for example this: https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/ea89d8d7e723a92601bbdb0cce89c28eaa30a5fc/platform/mcu/CMSIS/Device/ST/STM32F4xx/Include/stm32f405xx.h#L431 and https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/ea89d8d7e723a92601bbdb0cce89c28eaa30a5fc/platform/mcu/CMSIS/Device/ST/STM32F4xx/Include/stm32f405xx.h#L1001
Please create a gpio_hrc7000 driver and use it instead of the macros. You'll find some examples on how to do it here: https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/tree/master/platform/drivers/GPIO

+#define HRC7000_REGISTERS_H

+#include <stdint.h>

+/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ *  SOCSYS -- chip system control / clock / pin-mux (base 0x11000000)
+ *  Manual 4.1 (reset), 4.2 (clock), 4.4 (system control).
+ * ------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

+                                      * [4]codec [3]audio [2]fm [1]phy [0]protocol */

+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG08; /* 0x08 APLL divider configuration */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG0C; /* 0x0c APLL divider configuration */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG10; /* 0x10 BPLL divider configuration */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG14; /* 0x14 BPLL divider configuration */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG18; /* 0x18 baseband clock divider coefficient */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG1C; /* 0x1c FM 32K/192K divider coefficient */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG20; /* 0x20 codec I2S interface clock divider */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG24; /* 0x24 bus-related clock divider */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG28; /* 0x28 SDIO/USB clock divider */
+    volatile uint32_t CLK_MGR_REG2C; /* 0x2c gated-clock control enable */
+    volatile uint32_t LCSFC_BAUDR;   /* 0x30 LCSFC SPI SCLK clock divider */
+    volatile uint32_t IO_DIPLEX0;    /* 0x34 PTA pad mux (i2c1/uart2/audio) */
+    volatile uint32_t IO_DIPLEX1;    /* 0x38 PTA pad mux (spi0 pins) */
+    volatile uint32_t IO_DIPLEX2;    /* 0x3c PTC pad mux */

+ * ------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

+    volatile uint32_t DDR;     /* 0x04 direction: 1 = output (SWPORTA_DDR) */
+    uint32_t RESERVED0[10];    /* 0x08 - 0x2c */
+    volatile uint32_t INTEN;   /* 0x30 interrupt enable */
+    volatile uint32_t INTMASK; /* 0x34 interrupt mask */
+    volatile uint32_t INTTYPE_LEVEL; /* 0x38 interrupt type (edge/level) */
+    volatile uint32_t INT_POLARITY;  /* 0x3c interrupt polarity */
+    volatile uint32_t INTSTATUS;     /* 0x40 masked interrupt status */
+    volatile uint32_t RAW_INTSTATUS; /* 0x44 raw (pre-mask) interrupt status */
+    volatile uint32_t DEBOUNCE;      /* 0x48 debounce enable */
+    volatile uint32_t PORTA_EOI; /* 0x4c interrupt clear (end-of-interrupt) */
+    volatile uint32_t EXT_PORT;  /* 0x50 input read-back (EXT_PORTA) */

+/* GPIOB control/status bits (live-verified against V2.1.3). */
+#define LED_GREEN_BIT (1u << 0) /* PTB0,  active-high (also miosix ledOn) */
+#define LED_RED_BIT (1u << 1)   /* PTB1,  active-high */

+#define GPS_PWR_BIT (1u << 15)  /* PTB15, GPS module power: HIGH = on */
+
+/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------
+ *  LCD -- HR_C7000 hardware i8080 controller (base 0x12000000, manual 5.3)
+ * ------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
+typedef struct {
+    volatile uint32_t INDEX; /* 0x00 command cycle */
+    volatile uint32_t DATA;  /* 0x04 8-bit data cycle */
+    uint32_t RESERVED0[2];   /* 0x08 - 0x0c */
+    volatile uint32_t WCFG;  /* 0x10 write strobe timing */

There is no need for `adc_hd2_battery_raw_avg` because battery voltage is already filtered by the state update function.

feedback.body:
A couple of general comments:
- like the other targets, it'd be good to have a `pinmap.h` file where each GPIO is assigned a unique label specifying its function. Instead of having `gpio_readPin(GPIOB, 11)`, it is better to have `gpio_readPin(PTT_IN)`. See for example https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/master/platform/targets/MD-3x0/pinmap.h
- please remove all the implicit initialization paths like
```
    if (!rtc_ready)
        rtc_init()
 ```
A peripheral should be initialized only explicitly by calling its init function: if this does not happen, is a bug and it should cause side effects.
This function is almost equal to `adc_wait_busy`: probably it does make sense to have a single function which does both things based on a parameter.

replies.body:
The generic `adc_getRawSample()` wrapper in `peripherals/adc.h` already locks `adc->mutex` around the driver's `sample()`, so taking the lock inside `sample()` as well would double-lock it (the STM32F4 driver's `sample()` likewise doesn't lock for that reason).

The real bug this points at is that `adc1` was defined with a `NULL` mutex, so nothing was actually being serialized. Fixed: `adc1` now gets a real `pthread_mutex_t` (`adc1Mutex` in `hwconfig.c`, matching the CS7000 pattern), so the wrapper serializes concurrent conversions. Happy to move the lock into the driver instead if you'd prefer it there.

+ * "alternate-function B" selector (per-bank register at +0x78, outside the

replies.body: Kept as a separate hook for now. On this SoC the standard alternate-function/pad-mux selection goes through the SOCSYS `IO_DIPLEX*` registers, whereas `gpio_setMode(..., ALTERNATE)` maps to the DW_apb_gpio block's own mode bits. `gpio_setAltFuncB` pokes a bespoke per-bank vendor register at `+0x78` that's distinct from both, so folding it into `setMode(ALTERNATE)` would conflate two different mechanisms. Happy to revisit unifying them if you'd prefer.

The one residual is the `extern const hwInfo_t hwInfo;` you see here: `hwconfig.h` can't declare it, because `hwInfo_t` comes from `interfaces/platform.h`, and `platform.h` already includes `hwconfig.h` — so pulling `platform.h` into `hwconfig.h` creates an include cycle (which bit me: the `CONFIG_*`-gated decls in `platform.h` get skipped). feedback.body: If you can fix the rtx one as I suggested, it'd be nice. If it takes more than five minutes, ignore it and we keep these stubs as they are now and remove them in later PRs.
Note for future PRs: if possible, make each commit bisectable so that we can go back to them in case something does not work.

> I looked into wiring up the real rtx path (dropping the `rtx_*` stubs and adding `rtx.cpp` + `radio_stub.c`), but `rtx.cpp` instantiates `OpMode_FM` unconditionally and `OpMode_FM.cpp` calls `AT1846S::instance()` directly, so linking it pulls in the full AT1846S baseband + I2C1 HAL — exactly the scope this PR is trying to keep out.

Ouch! I'll need to remove this dependency, then.

> So I've kept the `rtx_*` (and `vp_*`) stubs in `hd2_core_stubs.c` for this PR. The FM branch that follows brings up the AT1846S HAL + OpMode_FM properly and clears the `rtx_*` stubs; the ADPCM/codec2 voice-prompt branches clear the `vp_*` ones.

Looks good to me!

> One upstream thought while I was in there: `fmMode` is instantiated unconditionally in `rtx.cpp` (only `m17Mode` is config-gated). If `fmMode` were gated the same way, a radio could link the rtx stack without a baseband driver. Happy to open that as a separate change if it'd be useful.

Indeed, FM mode should be gated as well. There are targets like Module17 which do not support FM and it does not make sense to have it enabled there.
Thank you!

replies.body:
I'm not sure this makes sense for HDLC. I'm not as knowledgeable about M17, but it looks like it has distinct states in the demodulator, SYNCED, INIT.

HDLC is really just always counting ones and IF there are six of them it's a flag. If there's five of them and a zero you ignore it (it's been stuffed in there to avoid a flag), if there's seven, something went wrong. 

To implement a switch statement you would need some logic to set the state based on what bit was received and how many ones have been counted (basically what's in there already) and then you'd take actions. I'm not sure it would be any more readable than comments in the if statements.

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
Just FYI, I wanted to test the FIR implementation to see if there was any benefit to doing it in blocks with overlap-add the way I implemented it, or doing it one at a time like OpenRTX currently has. Long story short, for an 81 tap FIR used to do the RRC calculation on a 1920 sample block (like you're currently using in the M17 code) there really isn't any noticeable benefit.

I put [my test](https://github.com/rxt1077/OpenRTX/blob/27fd914ff6975d93a2f90d81a251ef29c2e6227b/tests/unit/FIR.cpp) and [FIR implementation](https://github.com/rxt1077/OpenRTX/blob/27fd914ff6975d93a2f90d81a251ef29c2e6227b/openrtx/include/core/fir.hpp) in a separate branch, [fir-test](https://github.com/rxt1077/OpenRTX/tree/fir-test). You may be able to [eek out some more performance from that convolution in a similar fashion using an FFT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overlap%E2%80%93add_method).

Other things to consider are whether that FIR code can be modified/made more generic and used in the correlation work you do for sync symbols. I think there's also some ARM-optimized convolution functions from CMSIS-DSP I saw reference is the Miosix kernel.

This is really a long winded way of saying I haven't forgotten about this and I think the best solution is to add a type to the Fir class template, update the M17 code to use the float type when setting up that class, and modify the APRS code to use the Fir class too, which I realize is exactly what you asked for!

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
OK, I've finished switching over to using the FIR code currently in OpenRTX. I refactored the way Demodulator, Slicer, and Decoder work to match the way Fir works, namely to operate on one sample at a time and use operator() since they're all basically a class that does one thing. This makes things simpler: less bit packing and unpacking, Decoder will now emit _one_ frame or nothing, no need for a vector of frames. The OpMode and test had to be refactored as well.

In the process I also fixed a missing test case (no packets decoded) and a memory leak in Decoder (currentFrame needs to be freed if the program ends before we get the final flag).

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
I actually think they all belong as member functions in _APRS::Demodulator_ and the _APRS::Slicer_ and _APRS::Decoder_ classes should be scrapped. Here's why:

1. _APRS::Demodulator_ will be handling the _readyFrame_ and _demodFrame_ pointers to store frames that go to OpMode_APRS. If I put an instance of _APRS::Decoder_ class inside _APRS::Demodulator_ I'd have to deal with moving or referencing those pointers from a class within a class. If I take out the _decode_ function (operator() in _APRS::Decoder_ right now) and put it directly in the _APRS::Demodulator_ class I can deal with it more directly and the net effect is OpMode_APRS still looks neater.
1. Eventually we'll need to pull signals from other parts of the whole process to notify OpMode_APRS of what's going on. For example, digital carrier detection is usually pulled from the state of clock recovery which right now is inside _APRS::Slicer_. If I move the _slice_ function (operator() in APRS::Slicer) into _APRS::Demodulator_ I can get at that signal more directly. The same holds true to signaling when a packet fails a CRC.

I realize the down side is that _APRS::Demodulator_ gets harder to look at, but if you take it member funtion-by-function it's not too bad. It does have to maintain variables for state across the demodulator, slicer, and decoder but all-in-all that's 9 variables or so.

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
I think having the _Demodulator_ spit out the data portion of an HDLC frame would be our best bet. Unfortunately HDLC requires bit unstuffing, HDLC flag removal, and LSB to MSB conversion just to check the Frame Check Sequence (CRC). You pretty much have to decode it to know if you've received a valid frame.

The good news is this gives you some flexibility. You could take that data and wrap it in a KISS frame to make a TNC or you could interpret it as an APRS/AX.25 packet.

We'll need double buffering if _Demodulator_ operates in chunks since you could close out one frame and start the next within the chunk you're processing.

Having tried the monolithic class technique I originally proposed, I'm now of the opinion that we should still have a _Decoder_ and _Slicer_ class within _Demodulator_ (like you proposed). It's just too hard to look at otherwise.

I've rewritten the _Decoder_ to make it easier to understand, based on some of your earlier comments regarding using an FSM. I now break things down into states acting on signals from the bit counter. I think it reads easier and addresses some of the obvious comments issues.

I should finish this refactor soon.

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
So to be specific with the terminology the modulation is AFSK (keying being a special form of modulation) on top of FM (also modulation). A chip on the radio already handles the FM demodulation for us and gives us base band audio. If we are demodulating AFSK you'd usually ask for discriminator output, or the difference between tones. This is what _APRS::Demodulator_ as originally written gives you.

To get up to HDLC you need to recover bit timing and make bit decisions this is what _APRS::Slicer_ does. It's still just bits, no bytes yet. Finally you can decode it, _APRS::Decoder_, to get HDLC flags, unstuff bits, check CRCs, etc.

Unfortunately the term demodulation is a little overloaded and sometimes it's used to mean recovering frames from something that is digitally modulated.

So we could put those steps in some overarching class: Demodulation -> Slicing -> Decoding, technically with a little signal conditioning before the Demodulation step (removing DC). I originally put those steps in OpMode_APRS (which made it a little busy).

If you really want an HDLC frame, it would come out of an intermediary step in _APRS::Decoder_ where you've detected a frame by counting bits, but you didn't unstuff bits, correct endianness, or check the CRC.

feedback.body:
Yes, good points.
I was thinking that it'd be good to keep the HDLC framing outside the demodulator. The rationale for this is that you can reuse it in case there are devices capable of handling the demodulating part in hardware outputting raw frames. Is similar to what we do for M17: the demodulator outputs raw frames and then there is the frame decoder that does the rest.
The demodulator can return a reference to a raw frame, and this is passed to the HDLC layer, avoiding unnecessary copies.
We can probably avoid the double buffering, and having the demodulator doing nothing until the frame is read and acknowledged by the HDLC: we risk losing some frames, but probably we can afford this.
What do you think?

> I think having the _Demodulator_ spit out the data portion of an HDLC frame would be our best bet. Unfortunately HDLC requires bit unstuffing, HDLC flag removal, and LSB to MSB conversion just to check the Frame Check Sequence (CRC). You pretty much have to decode it to know if you've received a valid frame.

However this means that the demodulator has to do everything, comprised bit unstuffing, endianness conversion and CRC check. Or am I missing something?
What I proposed to do is to have the demodulator spitting out raw HDLC frames, that is everything between the two 0x7E markers, and then have a separate module that does the unstuffing and CRC validation. This would be similar to the M17 implementation, where we have the demodulator (which does not care about the content of the frames, except for the syncword) and then the frame decoder.
Sounds good!

replies.author: rxt1077
replies.body:
This isn't a raw HDLC frame. As far as I can tell there's a couple of issues with those that cause HDLC and AX.25 to be hopelessly intertwined in most implementations. This is just the data that is inside the HDLC frame which we already had to decode in the process.

In case you're interested, the HDLC/AX.25 issues that cause them to be linked are:

1. Frames are separated by one or more flags, but you don't know they're valid until you check the frame check sequence (CRC). You get a lot of spurious flags just listening to noise.
2. Checking the FCS (CRC) requires unstuffing the bits. Which requires working with the incoming signal bit by bit.
3. Watching for flags requires working with the incoming signal bit by bit.

It would be great if we could just have a decent indicator that we've received a flag and ship those bytes off to another layer for processing once one comes in. Unfortunately we have to do 90% of the work of the next layer just check to see if we've received a valid frame.

replies.body: The way I currently handle files is that I consider them corrupted if it is all zeroes. Because there is no "erase" function, I know this is a specific case and then I write 0xFF to the area so that the logic stays the same for all implementations. I am not sure how this would apply to eMMC. Do we have any example of a radio using raw eMMC device?

replies.author: mdiepart
replies.body:
I had a quick look. It looks like eMMC reads 0xFF partly because it uses flash memory for the physical support. This however made me think about how to handle "corrupted" memory. The only reason we *need* to erase memory before writing is in the cases where we can only erase a full page. Maybe the solution is to not erase memory when there is no erase function and just overwrite what is considered "corrupted". 
I'll implement that hopefully tomorrow. Maybe later down the road if we have an eMMC use case or rather a use case with memory that erases to 0x00, it will be time to see if something needs to be changed in either the settings API or the NVM API.
Does this seems good to you?

feedback.body:
From what I remember an erased eMMC reads all zeroes instead of 0xFFFF. Actually the intent of my comment was to make the implementation future-proof rather than covering an existing case.

About the fill with 0xFF: I re-read all the code and now I understand why you do so. It came to my mind a case where this is not very efficient, though: when the NVM storage is an I2C eeprom (like in GD-77 and DM-1801) the settings system is filling an entire block with 0xFF and immediately after it writes a valid entry at the top. Apart from taking some time, this spends extra write life of the eeprom memory itself every time a block needs to be erased.

If I understood all the logic correctly, we can probably change it to consider a partition either "valid" or "invalid", with the latter case being either a partition with corrupted data or a totally empty one. When writing to an invalid partition, then, it will be enough to directly write the new data block (preceded by an erase, if necessary) without the 0xFF fill.
The only downside of this approach that comes to my mind is that, when an already-erased flash memory is used, this will be considered invalid and erased again even if not necessary. This, however, should happen only the first time the code is run on the device. 

What do you think? I could have missed some important detail...

+        return 0;

+        return stale ? -1 : 1;

+/**
+ * \internal
+ * Parse an NVM partition and look for a settings structure. This function
+ * makes no guarantee that the store structure found is sound.
+ *
+ * @param dev NVM device to read from

+ * @param offset pointer that will contain the partition offset to the beginning
+ *               of the settings structure found. offset is invalid if the
+ *               function does not return 0.
+ * @param limit contains the maximum offset to explore within the partition
+ * @return 0 if successful, negative error code otherwise

feedback.body:
> I had a quick look. It looks like eMMC reads 0xFF partly because it uses flash memory for the physical support.

My bad, I thought eMMC had a different behavior. I got confused by the experience I had with one of those in the past.

> This however made me think about how to handle "corrupted" memory. The only reason we _need_ to erase memory before writing is in the cases where we can only erase a full page. Maybe the solution is to not erase memory when there is no erase function and just overwrite what is considered "corrupted". I'll implement that hopefully tomorrow.

Yes, that's my thought. When we do not need to erase memory, writing a new valid entry at the beginning of the page should be enough to make it again valid. All the old data below this new entry will be anyways overwritten over time.

> Maybe later down the road if we have an eMMC use case or rather a use case with memory that erases to 0x00, it will be time to see if something needs to be changed in either the settings API or the NVM API.

Yes, let's leave it for later. As Italian people say: "Don't bandage your head before breaking it". :smile:

Do we really need this `for` loop? `CODEC2_FRAME_SAMPLES` is divisible by two (and I never expect to have a codec requiring an odd number of samples) so, for any oversampling ratio, the number of samples returned by `inputStream_getData` will be an integer multiple of the oversampling ratio and we'll never fall "across" an unfinished block.
To be demonstrated, though.

I'd call this `CONFIG_CODEC_ENCODE_GAIN`: yes, now it is being used mainly for the microphone, but codec2 can accept any input stream.

feedback.body:
For the packet frame class:
 - let's call it `PacketFrame` without the "M17" prefix: we already did this for the metadata and, in the long term, we decided to remove the "M17" prefix from all the M17-related files and data structures (we already have the namespace for this);
 - instead of having the `payload` method returning a reference to the internal container, I'd implement the `operator []` like in [std::array](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/array/operator_at.html). This allows to do `packet[0] = 3;` instead of `packet.payload()[0] = 3;`
 - I'd replace the `getData` method with a `data` one like, again, in [std::array](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/array/data.html)
 
I'll do the same with the other M17 data structures to have everything uniform. We have to keep in mind that the current M17 implementation still contains some effects of the quick-and-dirty implementation I did in two weeks during the summer of 2022.
There is still the indent left over :)

+namespace M17

+/**
+ * This class describes and handles a generic M17 packet frame.
+ *
+ * The frame is 26 bytes on the wire: 25 bytes of packet data followed by a
+ * 1-byte metadata field (EOF flag, 5-bit counter, 2 reserved bits).
+ * Element access uses operator[] (like std::array); metadata is manipulated
+ * exclusively through setEof()/isEof()/setCounter()/getCounter().
+ */
+class PacketFrame
+{
+public:
+    static constexpr size_t DATA_SIZE = 25;
+    static constexpr size_t FRAME_SIZE = DATA_SIZE + 1; // 25 data + 1 metadata
+
+    /**
+     * Constructor.
+     */
+    PacketFrame()
+    {
+        clear();
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Clear the frame content, filling it with zeroes.
+     */
+    void clear()
+    {
+        frameData.payloadData.fill(0);
+        frameData.metadata = 0;
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Access a payload byte by index.
+     *
+     * @param index: byte position in the 25-byte data portion.
+     * @return a reference to the byte at the given index.
+     */
+    uint8_t &operator[](size_t index)
+    {
+        return frameData.payloadData[index];
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Access a payload byte by index (const overload).
+     *
+     * @param index: byte position in the 25-byte data portion.
+     * @return the byte value at the given index.
+     */
+    uint8_t operator[](size_t index) const
+    {
+        return frameData.payloadData[index];
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Set the EOF (last frame) flag.
+     *
+     * @param eof: true to mark this as the last packet frame.
+     */
+    void setEof(bool eof)
+    {
+        if (eof)
+            frameData.metadata |= EOF_BIT;
+        else
+            frameData.metadata &= ~EOF_BIT;
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Check if this is the last packet frame.
+     *
+     * @return true if the EOF bit is set.
+     */
+    bool isEof() const
+    {
+        return (frameData.metadata & EOF_BIT) != 0;
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Set the 5-bit counter field (bits 6..2 of byte 25).
+     *
+     * For intermediate frames (EOF=0) this is the frame sequence number.
+     * For the final frame (EOF=1) this is the number of valid data bytes
+     * in the last 25-byte chunk (1-25).
+     *
+     * @param counter: value between 0 and 31.
+     */
+    void setCounter(uint8_t counter)
+    {
+        frameData.metadata = (frameData.metadata & COUNTER_CLEAR)
+                           | ((counter & COUNTER_MASK) << COUNTER_SHIFT);
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Get the 5-bit counter field.
+     *
+     * @return counter value between 0 and 31.  See setCounter() for
+     * interpretation based on the EOF flag.
+     */
+    uint8_t getCounter() const
+    {
+        return (frameData.metadata >> COUNTER_SHIFT) & COUNTER_MASK;
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * Get underlying data (all 26 bytes: payload + metadata).
+     *
+     * @return a pointer to const uint8_t allowing direct access to frame data.
+     */
+    const uint8_t *data() const
+    {
+        return reinterpret_cast<const uint8_t *>(&frameData);
+    }
+
+private:
+    static constexpr uint8_t EOF_BIT = 0x80;
+    static constexpr uint8_t COUNTER_MASK = 0x1F;
+    static constexpr uint8_t COUNTER_SHIFT = 2;
+    static constexpr uint8_t COUNTER_CLEAR =

feedback.body:
> I mainly renamed STM32Flash to internalFlash.

I'd have kept it named `stm32Flash`, so that there is a reference to the target device. Actually, I'd change the prefix of the function names to `flashStm32`: we already have `spiStm32` and `adcStm32` in the drivers, so I'd go on with this convention for consistency.

> I then moved the two copies of flash.h to peripherals/flash.h. I also added two variables to stm32yyyxxx/flash.c instead of internal_flash.c.

> There is a lot of common code for the logic of the internal flash itself, should it stay in the header file?

From the partial reorganization you did, I can see that in the end the common code is around 70 lines: I think we can just have it duplicated in the two implementation files and call it a day.

So, I'd go for a common header file and two different implementations for each MCU family. This allows also for some optimizations: for example in the case of the STM32H7 the function performing bounds checking on the address can be reduced to checking only if the address is above or below the address range.

> I had to remove the const specifier to some nvm structs and deciced to remove them all. I don't think it makes that much sense to keep them and it makes it impossible to have reasonably flexible code without massive code deduplication.

The NVM structs have to be `const` actually: the reason is that, by doing so, their instances end up in the `.rodata` area which resides in flash memory. Given that in the 99% of the cases the data contained in those structs will never change, is better to not "waste" RAM space for them.

You can have const pointers to structs and still be able to change their fields. I'm already doing this in the zephyr flash driver: https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/b262fd5fe1e1959c53f24d39cc08b8b8b9920941/platform/drivers/NVM/flash_zephyr.h#L29 https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/b262fd5fe1e1959c53f24d39cc08b8b8b9920941/platform/drivers/NVM/flash_zephyr.c#L32

To handle the additional information for the STM32F4 flash, I'd do the following:
```
#define INTERNAL_FLASH_DEVICE_DEFINE(name)        \
    static struct nvmInfo name##_nvmInfo;         \
    static struct internalFlashArea name##_priv;  \
    static struct nvmDevice name = {              \
        .priv = &name##_priv,                     \
        .ops = &internalFlash_ops,                \
        .info = &name##_nvmInfo,                  \
     };
```
and then fill the fields of `priv` in the initialization function.

Another option is to go back to the `enum` for sector sizes and have something like this:
```
enum sectorSize {
    SECTOR_SIZE_16K
    SECTOR_SIZE_64K
    SECTOR_SIZE_128K
};

#define INTERNAL_FLASH_DEVICE_DEFINE(name, sector_size)        \
    static struct nvmInfo name##_nvmInfo;         \
    static struct nvmDevice name = {              \
        .priv = (const void *) sector_size,                     \
        .ops = &internalFlash_ops,                \
        .info = &name##_nvmInfo,                  \
     };
```
and then use `dev->priv` as the index into the array of `struct internalFlashArea`. For STM32H7 this will be unused, but this detail is hidden into the implementation file.

I'd say, let's make the header file device-specific for STM32. We also have to take into account that other MCUs may have different ways to access and manage the internal flash memory, so we'll probably end up having a set of device-specific drivers in any case.
Another thing that I forgot to mention, is that I'd like to move all the drivers that can be directly instantiated from OpenRTX main codebase into the `platform/drivers` folder.

> Ok, let's step back and make sure of what to do. I have two PR waiting to be reviewed and I can't afford to rewrite each PR three times to change the angle of attack, change the features set, or handle hypothetical use cases.
> 
> This PR was initially mainly for Module17 to store settings using the current nvm driver. I thus created a driver for the internal flash of that MCU (that covers more than half the OpenRTX devices). I also added support for STM32H743 because this was a low-hanging fruit. Then I had to make the header device generic which is a major PITA because of all the const values everywhere in the storage driver. Now I need to make the header device specific and we are talking about supporting MCUs that, for now, don't need this driver.
> 
> I say, we fix minor issues about this driver and move on. Later down the road, if we need to support additional devices, we will see if it requires making the driver device specific. It will probably not because the header file contains basically nothing except for the type of driver and the sector size (which is generic enough).

Acyually in my mind the plan was to go just for an STM32F4-specific driver to minimize the effort, but I wasn't clear in telling that.
Sorry for the mess and thanks for the patience. ❤️

> Ok, only thing left:
> 
> Should we rewrite the MDx/Mod17 nvmem api to use this one? Those two devices are the only reason I left the original flash.h/flash.c files.

I'd say no. When the new setting system is deployed, we move everything to the new API and then cleanup all the old files

> It's all good. However I tried running the platform tests and something is wrong. I'm glad I wrote them but now I'm trying to debug whatever is happening.

I can take care of it, if you want

feedback.body:
The chained `if` clauses processing the content of the metadata field makes me think that, probably, we have to first refactor how the metadata as a whole is managed.
To do so, I believe we should introduce a `Metadata` class representing the generic M17 metadata containing the raw bytes and a type field providing information on how to interpret the content. The LSF class should not care about what the metadata content is except for the type flag (too bad that the information is scattered around all the LSF block, preventing us from adopting a more clean approach). Then, should we subclass the `Metadata` to have a specific class for each metadata type? Or should we stick to have a single class with multiple methods?
Actually this is a case where `dynamic_cast` and RTTI can be helpful, if they're not too heavy.
Given that features like gnss and meta text are more of the _nice to have_ type, I believe we can take the occasion to introduce substantial code improvements alongside with them.

Don't hate me, but I think is cleaner to convert the code in this file to a C++ class. In the end the `MetaTextState` is basically a class without being `class`.
Also, for meta text reassembly, there is no real need of storing each block _and_ the final string: you can just have the character buffer and an `uint8_t` with the bitmap of the blocks added. The M17 specification provides an hint:
```
The Control Byte is split into two 4-bit fields. The most significant four bits are a bit map of
the message length indicating how many Text Data blocks are required for a complete message.
[...]
The least significant four bits indicate which of the Text Data blocks this text corresponds to.
[...]
Any received Control Byte is OR-ed together by the receiving station, and once the most significant
and least significant four bits are the same, a complete message has been received.
```

The `strncpy(status->M17_src, src, 10)` can be moved to line 202 and done only once.
The code was as it was to avoid copying into `status->M17_src` twice in case the LSF metadata contained an extended callsign, but in the end doing otherwise does not really make any difference.
A `switch` statement instead of a chain of `if`s is probably easier to read

The value returned by `getTick` is monotonically increasing, there is no real need to reset `m17_meta_text_last_scroll_tick` each time. Because of this you can also replace all the `meta_text_was_empty = true` lines with just `m17_meta_text_scroll_position = 0` and simplify the code a little bit.

Is not prohibited to add them now :)
This PR introduces the full MetaText class _and_ the RX functionality, while the next one will add the necessary glue code for TX

I think making the tx metatext value non-persistent would be confusing and unintuitive to the user, since they set this from the settings menu alongside other things that do get persisted. Making this non-persistent would require  moving the menu entry out of settings page and into the new vfo settings page.

replies.author: turnrye
replies.body:
Meta text would be something set independently of the memory channel, but still a persistent setting. I'd imagine that having one value is fine for now, and a potential future enhancement would be to let the user predefine multiple values and then select from them. I would expect a similar capability for APRS status text as well. My rationale here is, if we take a comparative analysis, we identify these similar features on other modes:

- APRS with its comment status fields (both as a part of the mic-e definition and the standalone status; see [APRS Protocol Ref 1.0](https://www.aprs.org/doc/APRS101.PDF) Chapters 10 and 16)
- DStar has a 4 character "Note" field that is associated with the station callsign, often used to indicate a status or distinguish between multiple radios. There is also a TX Message option for a 20-char text field that is sent in the background during voice transmissions, which users often use to include things like name and location

To look into how these are treated in UIs, lets take a couple of examples. 

For D-star: For the ID-5100 which is a large touchscreen display, the user is able to specify 5 message options. They are able to select from these as they use the radio regardless of vfo or memory mode (see [p. 7-2 - p. 7-4](https://static.dxengineering.com/global/images/instructions/ico-id-5100a-d.pdf)). The ID-52a, which is an HT, has a similar treatment (see [p. 5-17](https://www.icomeurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/ID-52A_E_PLUS_ENG_AM_0.pdf)).

For APRS: The TH-D75 is a well-regarded APRS capable HT, which allows the sending of position comments. The user is able to select from 8 predefined or 7 custom position comments. Additionally, there is a status text menu option that permits specifying up to 5 comments, with one selected at a time to be included in beacons. In general, the radio treats these as mode settings, and they are set separately from the memory channel (see p. [14-3](https://kasc.kenwood.com/files/prod/3692/5/THD75E_User_manuals_English.pdf)).

feedback.body:
Hi!
Thanks for the PR! About the current clang-format configuration: I started working on a version more adherent to the code stile of the OpenRTX codebase but, due to lack of time, I never manage to complete it (also because fine-tuning everything is a long process). I have to search where I left the modified file and attach it here.

Btw, something I tried to configure is to avoid the linter aggressively reorder the whitespaces in the struct definitions. For example [this file](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/master/openrtx/include/calibration/calibInfo_GDx.h) became [this](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/75b2ae8845d87ede6ebc9a0a27244cc1925a09a2/openrtx/include/calibration/calibInfo_GDx.h) after a lint pass, something I consider a regression in the code style. If you know a wayt to tell clang-format to not bother with these alignment, please let me know.

Here you are the clang-format file I began to tweak. As you'll see, I set the `PenaltyBreakComment` to an insanely high value to prevent the lint to break a line when the comment overflows the 80 line limit by some characters. Rationale for this is:
1) comments are... comments, I don't consider it crucial to have them fall within the 80 column limit;
2) there are places where the lint pass makes the code worse than before because it breaks the line in an insane place, like [here](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/75b2ae8845d87ede6ebc9a0a27244cc1925a09a2/openrtx/include/calibration/calibInfo_GDx.h#L84) (before it was [this](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/e689e2f7ae53f15c2828bc5edeb8ed801ddd8050/openrtx/include/calibration/calibInfo_GDx.h#L84)).
 
Thanks for the work done so far!
[clang-format.txt](https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/files/12361711/clang-format.txt)

Is there a way to avoid having the lint doing this? Ok that the line goes above the 80 column limit, but breaking it like this make it unreadable. Probably the only way to fix this behavior is to split the comment (but geez).
We should prevent the lint from doing this

I'd really like to find a way to prevent clang-format from playing shenanigans like this
```
typedef struct {
    bandCalData_t
        data[2]; // Calibration data for VHF (index 0) and UHF (index 1) bands
    freq_t vhfCalPoints
        [8];     // VHF calibration points for both TX power and mod1Amplitude
    freq_t uhfPwrCalPoints[16]; // UHF calibration points for TX power
    freq_t uhfCalPoints[8];     // UHF calibration points for mod1Amplitude
} gdxCalibration_t;
```

The workaround is to set `ColumnLimit` to something a bit more than 80, like 100. Otherwise, I don't know if there is a way to tell clang-format to not break a like if the comment goes out of the column limit.

> Ok, I can undo that part. Let's document a strategy then for how we'll work towards getting the whole project formatted and tackle that as a follow-up.

Thanks!

> The CI just verifies that all of the code is formatted. It is not making code changes. The goal is to use CI to indicate if the project is properly formatted or not. We can't do this in the same way due to the changes you've requested in observation 2, but perhaps we can find a way to incrementally validate as part of that. I've put my suggestions in #346.

Ah, ok. I thought it had a more invasive approach. If the format doesn't pass, the CI rises an error? If we can choose between an error and a warning, I'd probably choose the latter

> How frequent is this? May want to change our convention for comment placement or disable formatting for this section. Edit: my searching also yields that there isn't a solution, and it seems like the best alternative is to shift comments to their own line in this scenario.

Is not very frequent, actually. We can just `clang-format off` these cases and call it a day

```
#define ZEPHYR_FLASH_DEVICE_DEFINE(name, alias, sz) \
static struct nvmInfo nvm_devInfo_##name;           \
static const struct nvmDevice name =                \
{                                                   \

    .ops    = &zephyr_flash_ops,                    \
    .info   = &nvm_devInfo_##name,                  \

};
```

feedback.body:
In the next days I'll add an `rtx_squelchStatus()` function returning true when the squelch is open.
Meanwhile I'm thinking where is the best place to put the backlight logic: probably we can put it temporarily in the keyboard task because of its 40Hz update rate.
As a general implementation I'd put a downcounter in the global state, decremented by one at each round by the state task, which ticks at 1Hz. PTT press and squelch opening turn on the backlight and set the counter to the timeout value then, when it reaches zero, the backlight is turned off.

Another point in favor of putting the backlight logic inside the keyboard task: in this way you can "trap" the keypress event and do not transmit it to the UI thread if the backlight is off. That is, the first press on any button with backlight off only turns on the backlight.
I added the `rtx_rxSquelchOpen()` API function, allowing to query the current status of the RX audio squelch
Keep it as it is now, we're not super-strict about those things!

feedback.body:
Super, thank you!
Can you tell briefly what was wrong with SDL events?

Good to know, thanks!
Indeed, on Linux we never had such an issue and, consequently, this problem went ahead silently. I think that there is no problem in spawning a dedicated thread which handles both SDL render and SDL keyboard events: one can allocate an intermediate framebuffer and use a condition variable to signal that a new render operation is needed. On the other hand, the thread can push keypresses to a circular buffer being read by the `keyboard_getKeys` function.
At least it can work as a bridge solution until we perform an extensive refactoring of the codebase (already planned) which will merge into a single thread the UI, state and keyboard management.

I just have to ask you three little things:
- replace tabs with four spaces
- to provide a bit of documentation for the `chan` functions following the doxygen style
- to uniform the code style to the one of the rest of the codebase, with Allman bracing.

Some guidelines can be found here: https://github.com/OpenRTX/openrtx.github.io/blob/master/coding_style.md
Don't get too much crazy at uniforming all the code style, update only your parts.

Thanks! :)
